articles.title: Nvidia rebounds after $480 billion wipeout
articles.summary: Nvidia stock (NVDA) surged nearly 4% in premarket trading on Wednesday, November 11, as investors bought the dip after a two-day sell-off that wiped roughly $480 billion from the chipmaker's market value. Shares rose to $175.45 at 6:49 a.m. ET, up 3.88%, after closing Tuesday at $168.89, down $9.78, or 5.47%.The rebound came alongside gains in US stock futures, with Nasdaq 100 futures rising 1.67%, S&P 500 futures gaining 0.74% and Dow futures edging up 0.03%.Investors are returning to AI stocks even as Nvidia faces an investigation involving CEO Jensen Huang, just six days before its November 17 earnings report.Why is Nvidia stock rising today after a $480 billion market value crash?Nvidia's rebound comes after two difficult trading sessions. Shares fell 4.3% on Monday and another 5.47% on Tuesday as investors reacted to reports about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of having links to Chinese intelligence.The stock closed Monday at $178.67 before falling to $168.89 on Tuesday. Wednesday's premarket recovery has helped Nvidia regain part of those losses, although shares remain below their level before the controversy intensified.The recovery is also part of a broader rally in AI stocks. CoreWeave shares gained more than 10% in premarket trading after its quarterly results helped ease concerns about AI infrastructure spending. Micron and Marvell also rose nearly 7%.Nvidia faces Jensen Huang investigation as board hires outside law firmNvidia confirmed on Tuesday that its independent directors had hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or US national security had been compromised.The investigation will be led by former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim.The company had already announced an independent review on Sunday. Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe that company secrets or national security had been compromised. It also expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.The allegations remain unproven, and China has denied claims of an espionage operation.Huang returned to Nvidia's office on Monday and continued holding meetings on Tuesday, according to CNBC. His return comes as investors assess whether the controversy could affect Nvidia's operations or leadership.Bank of America warns Nvidia could face three different outcomesBank of America outlined three possible scenarios for Nvidia in a research note on Tuesday.The first involves a contained investigation with no major disruption to leadership. Under this outcome, investor attention could return to Nvidia's earnings and AI chip demand.The second involves prolonged uncertainty that puts pressure on the company's valuation ahead of its quarterly results.The third carries greater financial risks. Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya warned that adverse findings, leadership changes or tighter restrictions could require investors to reassess Nvidia's earnings outlook.Morgan Stanley removes Nvidia stock from top picks after 25% declineMorgan Stanley removed Nvidia from its top stock picks on Wednesday after shares dropped more than 25% since the bank added the company to its list on October 2.The bank's analysts said Huang's leadership remains crucial to Nvidia's strategic direction.The decision adds to concerns about how much Nvidia's market valuation depends on its chief executive.Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank also warned that investors were concerned about possible additional US restrictions and further developments in the investigation.Speaking to CNBC, Blank said the situation was negative for Nvidia, Huang and the broader AI trade.Nvidia earnings on November 17: Can NVDA stock sustain its recovery?Nvidia's next quarterly earnings report is scheduled for November 17, giving investors another major event to watch.The market will focus on revenue growth, AI chip demand, profit margins and the company's guidance for the coming quarter.

articles.title: China builds inside Europe's walls
articles.summary: Sofia: China doesn't need to clear Europe's trade barriers. It can build inside them.Chinese companies are establishing production and supplier networks across Central and Eastern Europe, which could enable them to gain more control over the technologies and inputs that European manufacturing needs.China is increasingly challenging the European Union in the advanced manufacturing sectors that helped the EU weather the first China shock, which reshaped global manufacturing in the 2000s. Chinese firms are competing with the EU in chemicals, machinery, advanced equipment and autos - and increasingly coming out on top on both price and quality.The EU trade deficit with China has nearly quadrupled over the past decade, from around €100 billion in 2014 to over €370 billion in 2025, or roughly €1 billion a day, according to Eurostat data.France and Germany are seeking to push back with stronger trade defences, but import curbs will achieve little if Chinese investment, ownership and control of critical technologies recreates the same vulnerabilities inside the single market.LOOKING EASTCentral and Eastern Europe appear to be key to China's growth strategy in Europe.While the EU's trade deficit with China has hovered around 2% of EU gross domestic product (GDP) since 2014, it has risen sharply in parts of CEE. For example, Slovenia's goods deficit with China rose from 2.5% to 16% over that period. Meanwhile, Poland's goods deficit surged from €8.9 billion to €34.3 billion, equivalent to about 5.2% of GDP. The Czech Republic's deficit nearly quadrupled to €22 billion, or roughly 8% of GDP, and Hungary's tripled to €10.4 billion, or about 6% of GDP.Investment and corporate ties deepened that exposure. In 2025, Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) flows into the EU approached €16.8 billion, and the cumulative value of Chinese investment in the bloc was about €95 billion, according to Eurostat and Rhodium Group data.While most legacy Chinese FDI in Europe centered on Germany, France and the Benelux countries, the focus has shifted east in recent years. CEE has attracted more than half of Chinese FDI into the EU and Britain since 2021, according to an analysis by the Rhodium Group, with an even larger regional share when the Western Balkans are included. Hungary has attracted the largest share of new investment since the COVID-19 pandemic, hitting 44% in 2023 and 23% in 2025.The investment surge in CEE has largely been driven by mega-projects in the electric vehicle (EV) supply chain. Chinese EV and battery manufacturers CATL, BYD and Sunwoda are all establishing major Hungarian operations. Slovakia has attracted investment from Chinese battery tech firm Gotion, and will be the site of a new Volvo plant owned by the Chinese automaker Geely.Meanwhile, Serbia, which has significant steel and copper assets, has signed contracts with Chinese auto firms Minth , Shanghai Automotive Chassis (SHAC), BMTS Technology and Xingyu Automotive, envisaging around €1 billion in investment and nearly 1,700 car-parts jobs, according to the government. The deals also include a new robotics factory in Sabac, billed as Europe's first humanoid robot mass production base.These investments can create jobs, spur growth, and accelerate the energy transition, but they may also erode EU competitiveness over time. Outsourcing key advanced manufacturing technologies to Chinese entities risks deepening Europe's dependence on external supply chains and weakening domestic innovation and R&D.DEFEND, THEN COMPETEEurope is seeking to limit China's access to its consumer markets and industries, but the current Franco-German push for faster defensive trade action and tougher investment screening across the bloc appears to be too little too late.Europe's flagship proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, leaves manufacturers' key competitiveness gaps unaddressed. Moreover, its screening mechanism would largely leave unexamined Chinese control via ultimate ownership, foreign subsidies and supply-chain concentration - some key issues when looking at CEE's growing dependence.There is also the problem of fragmentation across the bloc. Investment deals might be in one country's interest but could weaken the bloc's collective negotiating position with Beijing. To address this, the continent would likely need a permanent European economic security coordination mechanism to unite trade, competition and national screening authorities that could identify risks before investments become irreversible.Yet the chances of forming such a body at a time of growing political fragmentation within EU countries seem slim.And, ultimately, protectionism can only get Europe so far. It cannot compensate for the region's structural problems, including expensive energy, fragmented capital markets and slow industrial innovation. For that, the region would likely need to create a true energy union and invest in technological innovation. Building trade walls buys time, but not true change.(The views expressed here are those of Martin Vladimirov, director of the Geoeconomics Program of the Center for the Study of Democracy (CSD))

articles.summary: IndiGo has extended the suspension of commercial flights to four destinations in Saudi Arabia amid continuing safety and security concerns, with services to Jeddah and Madinah halted until November 21 and those to Riyadh and Dammam suspended until November 30, 2026.The airline announced the extension in a travel advisory on social media platform X on November 10, stating that the decision followed a review of the prevailing security situation."Following a careful assessment of the safety and security considerations, IndiGo has further extended the suspension of flights to and from Jeddah and Madinah until 21 November 2026 (inclusive), and Riyadh and Dammam until 30 November 2026 (inclusive)," the airline announced in its advisory.IndiGo said it was contacting affected passengers through the details provided during booking. Customers are being informed about ticket re-accommodation, refunds and alternative travel arrangements."Timely notifications are being sent to affected customers using the contact details provided at the time of booking. We remain committed to keeping our customers informed and extending the necessary assistance during this period," the airline said.— IndiGo6E (@IndiGo6E) Reiterating its position on passenger and crew safety, the airline added, "The safety and security of our customers and crew remain our highest priority. We continue to closely monitor the situation and will share further updates as necessary."The extension comes amid renewed hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi rebels following the breakdown of a 2022 truce that had paused fighting in the country's prolonged civil war. The Houthis have previously targeted Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military installations.On November 8, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy confirmed that an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been targeted in an attempted attack.An official source at the ministry said falling shrapnel caused minor damage to the building. No injuries or fatalities were reported."The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported, thankfully," the source stated.Also read: UAE flight cancellations continue as airlines suspend Saudi routes until November 19"The source added that the relevant authorities promptly responded to the incident and took the necessary measures," the ministry's statement added.The incident followed claims by Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree that the group had conducted six military operations targeting strategic and military installations across Saudi Arabia using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.Saree claimed that the first operation targeted King Khalid International Airport, oil storage tanks and an Aramco distillation tower in Riyadh."The first operation targeted Khalid International Airport, oil storage tanks, and a distillation tower belonging to Aramco in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, and, by Allah's grace, successfully achieved its objective," Saree said.He also claimed that subsequent operations targeted Aramco facilities in Khurais, Pumping Station No. 8 in Dawadmi, a National Guard camp in Najran and troop positions east of Al-Jawf Governorate.The airline has not announced any further changes to the suspension dates.

The losses show that the market recovery has left behind a substantial number of companies across technology, pharmaceuticals, engineering, manufacturing and other sectors.For investors holding these stocks, the sharp improvement in benchmark indices has done little to offset the damage suffered during the broader market correction.Why is Nifty rising while smallcaps struggle?Apurva Sheth, Head of Market Perspectives and Research at SAMCO Securities, believes the divergence comes down to buying being concentrated in a handful of heavyweight stocks."A lot of investors are scratching their heads thinking why their portfolio isn't moving up with Nifty. The simple answer is you don't own what is moving up," Sheth said.According to his analysis, the Nifty Top 10 Equal Weight Index gained 10.64% over the preceding month, while the Nifty Midcap 150 and Nifty Smallcap 250 indices each declined 2.74%. The Nifty Microcap 250 fell 5.32%.The first major reason behind the divergence is valuation. Several largecap stocks had suffered heavy losses during the market correction that began in January 2026, bringing their valuations to more attractive levels.This encouraged investors to return to established companies as crude oil prices eased and concerns about the global economic outlook moderated.Smaller companies, meanwhile, entered the correction with relatively elevated valuations following their earlier rallies. Investors have remained selective amid concerns about earnings visibility and the sustainability of growth.Foreign money is chasing large companiesThe second major factor is the return of foreign institutional investors. After months of sustained selling, overseas investors have begun deploying substantial capital into Indian equities, helping lift banking, technology, telecommunications and other heavyweight stocks.Foreign investors have bought more than $4.1 billion worth of Indian equities so far in November, according to Reuters, marking the strongest monthly inflow since September 2024. However, foreign institutions generally prefer large, liquid companies where they can deploy substantial amounts without significantly affecting share prices.This has benefited stocks such as ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, Infosys, Bharti Airtel and Reliance Industries. According to Sheth, ICICI Bank and Infosys each gained 16% over his one-month review period, while Bharti Airtel advanced 14.61%. Kotak Mahindra Bank rose 10.08%, HDFC Bank gained 10%, and Reliance Industries climbed 8.44%.The ten heavyweight stocks in his analysis delivered an average return of 10.19%, highlighting how concentrated the rebound has been.For smaller companies, the absence of similar institutional buying has limited the recovery despite improving sentiment across the broader market.Can the broader market catch up?The broader market has also faced pressure from stretched valuations, uneven earnings performance and reduced risk appetite following months of geopolitical uncertainty and high crude oil prices.Although the September-quarter earnings season has shown signs of improvement, investors are increasingly distinguishing between companies delivering sustainable profit growth and those whose earlier valuations were driven by aggressive expectations.The next test for Dalal Street will be whether sustained foreign inflows and stronger corporate earnings encourage buying beyond the largest companies.Disclosure: This article was written by Podishetti Akash, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. articles.summary: Myaing, Myanmar: Myanmar's small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry increasingly lucrative amidst the Middle East energy shock."As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us," said Htun Aung, a worker on an artisanal oil well in Myanmar's arid heartlands.Also read | Jensen Huang case: Nvidia CEO love affair scandal revives push for tougher US line on China"But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder," said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.Myanmar imports 90 percent of its fuel oil, official figures show, making it particularly vulnerable to supply issues caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.But the central region of Magway hosts a hardscrabble industry of domestic prospectors manning grimy derricks that squelch up crude oil in humble quantities.The area is dubbed "Anyar Dubai", associating the Anyar landscape with the oil boom Emirate, despite the pitiable $50 per week earned by workers like Htun Aung who spend their days drenched in foul crude run-off.With prices at Myanmar's petrol pumps nearly double what they were in late February, the underground "black gold" is an increasingly coveted prize of war.Also read | Trump's Iran war may be 'militarily' over, but economic siege still haunts"We just want to live in peace," said Htun Aung. "But now they strike from one side and the others strike from the other -- they keep attacking each other.""We've had to flee three, four, five times already," he added. "We run here, we run there. We fill up our motorbikes with fuel and run again."Digging inAllied pro-democracy rebels claim to have controlled oil fields in Magway's Myaing township since 2023, the third year of a nationwide civil war triggered by a coup.They patrol the dusty territory in a westward crook of the Irrawaddy river in ragtag columns and outfitted with rocket-propelled grenades, flak jackets, tote bags and flip-flops.Air and drone strikes in Myaing so far this year have already exceeded 2025's total, according to ACLED, a monitor that estimates more than 100,000 people have died since the putsch.Rebels shelter in foxholes, camouflaged among thousands of oil wells dug in an unregulated practice dating back centuries.Engine winches chug day and night, plunging plumbing tubes dozens of metres down boreholes before dragging them up filled with crude oil slurry.Prospectors pay landowners up to $3,500 to lease a spot to drill,one veteran said, with no guarantee they will hit oil.Some wells yield dribbles while others gush profit, filling tarpaulin-lined pits and barrels with oil hauled off to improvised refineries for processing into petrol and diesel."Anyar Dubai" has been "going viral" for its plentiful supply, said rebel spokesman Pyae Phyo Kyaw, at a time when Myanmar military-held areas have been rationing petrol.He touted recent offensives fending off military advances, but admitted being battered by counter-attacks."We see it primarily as an attempt to destroy what has been a strong supply route and source of revenue for us," said the 35-year-old, speaking under his real name.Myanmar's military could not be reached for comment.But in September, a month-long military operation claimed to have captured over 130 wells in Myaing and 735 more in neighbouring Pakokku township.Black marketScores of pro-democracy factions and ethnic minority armed groups are fighting the military over the 2021 coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi.As the war grinds on, all sides battle to fill war chests with the tax or trade of natural resources: gem mines, rare earth mineral deposits, gold or teak.Oil projects are not generally contested.The major ones are under staunch military guard, and on-the-books output is tiny by international standards -- around 6,000 barrels a day last year, according to the US Energy Information Administration.But artisanal fields are coveted by rebels precisely because of their modest size, according to Thomas Kean, senior Myanmar consultant for the International Crisis Group."Part of the reason why they're significant is because they're not globally significant," he said, explaining that they are small enough to thrive under the radar, yet big enough to fund guerrillas.Spiking oil prices may not directly drive conflict, said Kean, highlighting a broader military campaign to evict rebels from heartland footholds by squeezing revenue sources.But as the spoils of war become more profitable, the stakes get higher."We're talking about millions of barrels a year coming out of these oil fields," he added."With global prices what they are, that's a significant amount of money."

Fed’s Christopher Waller opens door to 50-basis-point December rate hike after hot CPI
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller's remarks intensified the debate over a possible half-percentage-point interest-rate increase in December after US inflation data came in hotter than expected on Tuesday, Bloomberg reported.In a speech delivered in London before the release of October’s Consumer Price Index, Waller said he was inclined to support a rate increase in December. He warned that a 50-basis-point move might be necessary if inflation continued to accelerate, arguing that the Fed’s credibility could otherwise be at risk.Hours later, data showed that consumer prices rose more than expected. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% from the previous month, meeting the threshold Waller identified as grounds for considering a larger rate increase.Also read: Traders raise odds of 50 bps Fed rate hike as CPI rise exceeds expectationsWaller’s remarks represent the clearest signal yet from a Fed official that policymakers may need to raise rates in December by more than the quarter-percentage-point move markets had expected.Several senior Fed officials, including Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams, are scheduled to speak this week.Fed watchers said Waller’s comments did not make a 50-basis-point move certain but would add urgency to the debate over how aggressively policymakers must act to contain inflation.“This is not a print that screams out the need to go 50, but certainly provides ammunition to the argument to do so,” Christopher Hodge, chief US economist at Natixis, told Bloomberg.For live updates on US Markets, click hereTom Porcelli, chief economist at Wells Fargo, said he expected the Fed’s policy-setting committee to support another rate increase unanimously, although the size of the move remained open for debate.“This locks it down,” Porcelli said, referring to the likelihood of at least a 25-basis-point increase. “With Waller introducing that idea, the market is going to run with it in the face of this firm print.”Following Waller’s remarks and the inflation report, investors priced in a more aggressive path for interest rates in the coming months. However, markets remained unconvinced that policymakers would deliver a half-point increase in December.Federal funds futures continued to indicate a quarter-point move in December, followed by additional increases of the same size in January and possibly April. Investors had previously expected rate increases in December and March.Waller described the US economy as strong and the labour market as stable but said inflation remained too high.“If, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points,” Waller said.“But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3% or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed,” he added. “In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting.”Under such a scenario, Waller said a conventional quarter-point increase would do little to reassure the public that the Fed was serious about controlling inflation.“Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” he said.Also Read: Are days of easy money over? Aswath Damodaran warns of a new mkt realityHot CPI intensifies rate debateData released later by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that core consumer prices rose 0.3% in October from the previous month, while the headline CPI increased 0.4%.Fed officials held interest rates steady last month, saying the “accumulation of more information” would help them determine the appropriate policy setting.The 10-2 decision followed a unanimous vote in September to raise the benchmark rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75% to 4%. Several policymakers have since indicated that additional increases may be necessary.Data released last week showed that job growth accelerated in October while the unemployment rate edged lower. Fed officials will receive another employment report and a full set of inflation data before their December meeting.During a question-and-answer session with Bloomberg’s Francine Lacqua after the speech, Waller said the Fed did not want to “slam the economy down.”“It’s not that we’re going to jack up the policy rate 150 basis points or 200 basis points,” he said. “We are looking forward and saying we need to do something; at a minimum, probably take back the three insurance cuts that we put in last year.”Waller added that monetary policy had not been “nearly as restrictive as I thought it was.”(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

articles.title: Rupee set for another winning run?
articles.summary: The Indian rupee may appreciate further against the US dollar over the next couple of months, supported by easing global headwinds, declining crude oil prices, improving foreign capital inflows and a weakening US dollar, according to economists.Speaking to ANI, former UN adviser and economist Santosh Mehrotra said the domestic currency could strengthen further if the recent easing of global economic and geopolitical pressures continues."Overall, we can expect the Indian rupee to appreciate further over the coming couple of months," Mehrotra said, adding that the outlook would depend on whether global headwinds, which are currently subsiding, remain subdued or ease further.Explaining the factors behind the rupee's recent strengthening, Mehrotra said the Democrats' victory in both chambers of the US Congress had weakened the dollar by reducing the political and fiscal risk premium associated with the currency.He noted that the election outcome could make it more difficult for US President Donald Trump to push through his fiscal and spending agenda, potentially limiting fiscal expansion.Mehrotra also pointed to the possibility of de-escalation in the Middle East, which could reduce geopolitical risks and ease the risk premium in international crude oil prices.He said international crude prices, which were around USD 105 per barrel before the US election results, had declined to approximately USD 96 per barrel.With India importing around 90 per cent of its crude oil requirements, lower international oil prices could reduce the country's import bill and provide support to the domestic currency.Mehrotra also highlighted the return of foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to Indian equity markets as another factor supporting the rupee.He said foreign investors had purchased approximately USD 1 billion worth of Indian equities in November up to November 5, contributing to dollar inflows into the country.Additionally, he noted that the unwinding of investments in artificial intelligence-related stocks and technology companies in the US and North Asian economies could redirect capital towards other emerging markets, including India.Another supporting factor, according to Mehrotra, was the decline in US Treasury yields.He said US bond yields had eased from around 5.3 per cent to 5.2 per cent on the first day following the election results, as investors anticipated that a Democrat-controlled Congress could constrain Trump's fiscal expansion plans.Lower US Treasury yields could reduce the relative attractiveness of dollar-denominated assets and encourage investors to explore emerging-market bonds offering higher returns.Mehrotra added that Indian government securities had also benefited from improving market conditions, with yields declining by 11 basis points in November.Meanwhile, Devendra Pant, Chief Economist at India Ratings and Research Private Limited, told that declining crude oil prices, a narrowing gap between petroleum product and food prices, and the possibility of lower freight rates could further support the rupee.Pant said freight rates could ease if the announcement of no further US military activity in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding areas translated into a sustained reduction in regional tensions.He noted that these developments, alongside measures taken by the government and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to improve dollar availability, could help stabilise the domestic currency.These measures included the RBI directly providing dollars to oil marketing companies, reducing their need to purchase dollars from the market, along with measures relating to gold.Pant further highlighted that lower crude oil prices could moderate gas prices and ease pressure on the government's fertiliser subsidy bill, a major expenditure component that could otherwise affect fiscal calculations.He added that declining oil prices would also reduce the cost of petroleum imports compared with expectations prevailing a week or 10 days earlier.According to Pant, these developments could result in a lower-than-anticipated current account deficit, while capital inflows, particularly foreign portfolio investments, could improve.Asked about the extent of potential rupee appreciation, Pant said it was difficult to predict a specific level, although the overall outlook remained positive."I will not stick my neck out to give a number. The outlook is, you can say cautious optimism, and the rupee is likely to strengthen further," he said.However, Pant cautioned that any adverse geopolitical developments could reverse the currency's strengthening trend.He said that if the temporary truce or peace in the region holds, the rupee could appreciate further. Even in the event of depreciation, he expected the movement to remain orderly rather than witnessing the sharp declines seen over the past year or year and a half.Pant added that the global economic environment was showing signs of improvement, with headwinds originating in the Middle East gradually easing, a development that could benefit India's economy and international trade.

articles.title: India's water journey a model: WB official
articles.summary: United Nations: From bringing drinking water to millions of households to cleaning one of its most revered rivers, India's efforts to address its water challenges are increasingly drawing attention beyond its borders, with a senior World Bank official describing the initiatives as a model for developing nations."For the World Bank Group, India is a remarkable success story. It's the water journey that every single developing country is looking at," Saroj Kumar Jha, Global Director for Water at the World Bank Group, said in response to a PTI question during a virtual press briefing ahead of the 2026 United Nations Water Conference.Also Read: 2026 set to rank among four warmest years on record, says WMOThe recognition comes at a time when water security is increasingly becoming a global development priority, with countries grappling with the twin challenges of ensuring equitable access to clean water and protecting existing water resources from pollution and unsustainable use.Co-hosted by the United Arab Emirates and Senegal, the UN Water Conference will be held in Abu Dhabi from December 8 to 10.It will bring together world leaders, policymakers and other stakeholders to explore ways to strengthen international cooperation on water security and sanitation.Also Read: As Delhi gasps for clean air, parliamentary panel skips hearing on air pollutionFor Jha, India's experience offers something beyond ambitious targets and large-scale government programmes, a practical blueprint that other developing nations can adapt to their own circumstances.He highlighted several Indian initiatives, including the Jal Jeevan Mission, Namami Gange and Swachh Bharat Mission.Jha said during his recent visit to New Delhi and meetings with Indian government officials, he had encouraged them to use the international conference as a platform to share its experience and demonstrate how large-scale water management initiatives could be implemented."India has done what other countries are now trying to work on, and India offers the how-to part of the water solution," he said.Among the initiatives that have particularly impressed the World Bank is the Jal Jeevan Mission, which has sought to transform access to drinking water in rural India.Highlighting the scale of the programme, Jha said reaching 800 million people with improved drinking water access in less than seven years is a "remarkable" achievement.He described India's efforts to expand drinking water access in both urban and rural areas as "unprecedented", while pointing out that the programme is now evolving beyond expanding coverage to focus increasingly on sustainability, operations and maintenance.India's sanitation experience, too, has found resonance abroad. Jha cited Nigeria's 'Clean Nigeria' campaign as an initiative influenced by India's Swachh Bharat Mission."What India has done is already spreading to many other countries across the globe, and particularly countries in the South are looking at Jal Jeevan Mission as a good model to replicate with popular participation of people, government-strong leadership, adequate financing at all levels," he said.If access to drinking water and sanitation represents one dimension of India's water transformation, the effort to restore the health of its rivers represents another.Jha described the Namami Gange Programme as "remarkably successful" in reducing pollution in the Ganga and improving the overall health of the river.The World Bank has supported the National Mission for Clean Ganga through various financing instruments.For Jha, river conservation also has a significance that goes well beyond environmental protection."Rivers are not just rivers; they are part of our civilisation, part of the human system. People depend on these rivers for their livelihood," he said.The World Bank official also highlighted India's efforts to improve dam safety, saying the bank's funding had helped strengthen the resilience of nearly 900 dams. The establishment of centres of excellence has further helped build technical expertise and institutional capacity in the sector.India's urban water management initiatives also drew praise, particularly efforts to encourage creditworthy municipalities to tap capital markets and mobilise resources for improving civic water services.Jha acknowledged that India continued to face considerable challenges in water management, but said the progress made at both the central and state levels offered valuable lessons for other countries."We are looking at the entire system of water management in India... What they have done in this field is really remarkable, at the state level and the central government level," he said.India is expected to play an active role in the upcoming UN conference.Stephanie Rambler, Senior Sustainable Development Officer at the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, said the country is "very active" in preparations.India is expected to send a large high-level government delegation and organise a side event on 'river cities', focusing on water security and resilience, she said.The conference will feature seven plenary meetings and six interactive dialogues, besides special events aimed at accelerating progress towards Sustainable Development Goal 6, which seeks to ensure access to clean water and sanitation for all.

Russia, Ukraine first peace talks in 9 mths
articles.summary: Abu Dhabi: Russian and Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first US-brokered talks since February, after President Donald Trump suggested last week that a broad deal was possible on ending the war in Ukraine and guaranteeing security in Europe.US envoy Jared Kushner told delegates that recent contacts with both sides had "really identified, narrowed the gaps", and the US side had "some good ideas" on how to bridge their differences. Trump, he said, was committed to achieving peace.Also Read: US-mediated talks on ending Russia-Ukraine war begin in Abu Dhabi"He really has asked us to put extra effort into trying to find a solution that hopefully ends the war but also leaves both sides in a much stronger position" to realise their full potential, Kushner said.But more than 4-1/2 years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and with Russian forces holding about a fifth of the country, Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart - despite Trump's optimism - on terms for a possible settlement.Ukraine's chief delegate, Rustem Umerov, said in his opening remarks that Kyiv was focused on achieving security guarantees and a lasting peace.Also Read: Trump says Iran war's 'militarily' over, but US 'locked and loaded'Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov underlined Moscow's preference for negotiating a broad European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war."The idea of ​​defining clear parameters for a future security architecture, and only then moving on to resolving the actual Russia-Ukraine conflict, is absolutely reasonable," he told reporters in Moscow.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday voiced the opposite view, saying wider security talks should come only after a ceasefire in Ukraine. Lavrov again rejected the notion of a truce, saying the Europeans were trying to buy breathing space for Ukraine.Europeans seek a role in the processThe new American drive for a deal has galvanized European officials into pushing for a place at the table to seek an end to the continent's deadliest conflict since World War Two.Before the start of the main meeting, the Ukrainians met separately with European, NATO and EU representatives and the two American envoys, Kushner and Steve Witkoff.France said there could be no lasting peace in Ukraine without addressing European security, and that this required the involvement of the Europeans.Russia had made clear it did not see a place for Europeans at the meeting with the Ukrainians and Americans.On the eve of the talks, Trump said Washington was seeing a "very strong inclination" towards ending the war, and that both sides were "tired of fighting". After meeting privately with Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy last week at the White House, Trump predicted that a peace deal could emerge soon.Trump has frequently said an agreement was close, without a deal emerging. However, negotiations have picked up again in recent weeks after months in which Washington's attention was focused on the war in Iran.Publicly, there has been no sign that Putin is willing to drop his insistence that Ukraine surrender the entire eastern region of Donbas before a peace deal can be struck.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has refused to hand over land that his forces have died defending.Russian front-line advances have slowed to a virtual halt this year but Moscow has been pounding Ukrainian cities and energy facilities, while Ukraine has stepped up attacks on oil refineries and other infrastructure deep inside Russia.A source in the Russian delegation said Russia believed the main thrust of the talks would be trying to hammer out the key elements of a new post-war security framework for Europe.On the eve of the negotiations, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's leverage in the talks was increasing as a result of its recent battlefield performance, which has included retaking some territory in Donetsk, a coal-mining area of the Donbas."Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine's negotiating position," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address on Monday. He said Russia was suffering "record losses" - an assertion disputed by Moscow - and urged Washington to convince the Kremlin to end the war.US negotiators believe that Zelenskiy and Putin may be willing to strike a compromise on the vital question of territory, each ceding a little, a US official told Reuters.Under the proposed deal, Ukraine would get an end to the war, security guarantees and a roadmap to accession to the EU.A senior Ukrainian official strongly denied that the government would consider any such concessions. The issue of territory could be discussed only at the leaders' level and only in the context of appropriate security guarantees for Ukraine, the official said.
